Breed
breed
v.i. & n. (to bring forth young; a stock or race)
Old English bredan, to cherish or keep warm, hence to hatch. The Authorized Version uses the family for the multiplying of creatures after the flood, for a celebrated stock of rams, and for the breeding of nettles in a ruined land.

Biblical Definition

The word's first appearance is a commission given as the ark opened: “Bring forth with thee every living thing that is with thee, of all flesh, both of fowl, and of cattle, and of every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth; that they may breed abundantly in the earth, and be fruitful, and multiply upon the earth” (Genesis 8:17). Breeding here is not a blind biological fact but a charge: God renews the creation mandate to the beasts as well as to Noah. The noun names a stock in the song of Moses, where God's bounty to Israel is inventoried — “Butter of kine, and milk of sheep, with fat of lambs, and rams of the breed of Bashan” (Deuteronomy 32:14). And the participle names a curse: Zephaniah says Moab shall be “as Sodom, and the children of Ammon as Gomorrah, even the breeding of nettles, and saltpits, and a perpetual desolation” (Zephaniah 2:9). The same earth that breeds cattle abundantly breeds nettles where God has withdrawn; fruitfulness is a gift, not a property of the ground.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines breed as to procreate; to generate; to hatch; to produce; and as a noun, a race or progeny from the same stock.

expand to see more

BREED, v.t. To procreate; to generate; to beget; to hatch, as fowls do their young.

BREED, v.i. To produce, as a fetus; to bear and nourish, as in pregnancy.

BREED, n. A race or progeny from the same parents or stock.

BREED, n. A cast; a kind; a race of men or other animals which have an alliance by nativity.

MULTIPLY, v.i. To increase in number; to extend; to grow or become more numerous by propagation.

Key Scripture

Genesis 8:17 — "Bring forth with thee every living thing that is with thee, of all flesh, both of fowl, and of cattle, and of every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth; that they may breed abundantly in the earth, and be fruitful, and multiply upon the earth."

Deuteronomy 32:14 — "Butter of kine, and milk of sheep, with fat of lambs, and rams of the breed of Bashan, and goats, with the fat of kidneys of wheat; and thou didst drink the pure blood of the grape."

Zephaniah 2:9 — "Therefore as I live, saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, Surely Moab shall be as Sodom, and the children of Ammon as Gomorrah, even the breeding of nettles, and saltpits, and a perpetual desolation: the residue of my people shall spoil them, and the remnant of my people shall possess them."

Genesis 9:1 — "And God blessed Noah and his sons, and said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth."

Modern Corruption

Fruitfulness is now treated as a problem to be managed and multiplication as a threat to the planet, against a Bible in which breeding abundantly is a blessing commanded by God and barrenness of ground is the curse.

expand to see more

The dominant environmental account reverses Genesis 8. There multiplication is the aim, spoken over the beasts and then over Noah, and the earth's filling is the goal of the rescue rather than a danger created by it. The modern instinct treats human and animal increase alike as pressure on a finite system, and the corrective is not to deny finitude — Scripture is unsentimental about famine, drought and limits — but to refuse the premise that fruitfulness is itself the injury. God commanded the ark's creatures to breed abundantly in a world he had just emptied, and he called it good.

Zephaniah supplies the other half and keeps this from becoming naive. Ground can breed the wrong things. Moab and Ammon are sentenced to become the breeding of nettles and saltpits and a perpetual desolation, which is what a land does when God withdraws. Fruitfulness is therefore never a mechanism to be assumed but a mercy to be sought, and the recovery is stewardship under blessing: to keep and dress the earth as men who expect God to give the increase, and who know that the same soil grows nettles at his word.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sharats (H8317), to swarm or breed abundantly; parah (H6509), to be fruitful; rabah (H7235), to multiply; memshaq (H4476), a possession or breeding-place.

expand to see more

Hebrew sharats (H8317) — to swarm, to breed abundantly; the charge to the creatures in Genesis 8:17.

Hebrew parah (H6509) — to bear fruit, be fruitful; the first half of the creation mandate.

Hebrew rabah (H7235) — to become many, to multiply; the second half, renewed after the flood.

Hebrew ben (H1121) — son; behind rams of the breed, literally sons, of Bashan.

Hebrew charul (H2738) — the nettle; what a cursed ground breeds instead.

Usage

"“That they may breed abundantly in the earth” — a commission, not a danger."

"“Rams of the breed of Bashan” — God's bounty inventoried."

"“Even the breeding of nettles” — what ground yields under judgment."
